foundation.title: Your first local HTTP lab
foundation.brief: Serve one page on your own computer, request it with curl, then compare its successful response with a request for a page that does not exist.
steps:
Prepare two terminal windows on the computer where you will run this lab. We will call them Terminal A and Terminal B. Your workspace is open. Run the commands below in your terminals; Ascend does not execute them automatically.

In Terminal A, check that both tools are available:
```sh
python3 --version
curl --version
```
A Python 3 version and a curl version mean you can continue. If a tool is missing, end this session and use the first hint to repair your setup before continuing practice.

In Terminal A, make a new temporary folder containing one page, then serve that folder on your own computer: ```sh lab_site=$(mktemp -d /tmp/ascend-http.XXXXXX) printf '

My first lab

\n' > "$lab_site/index.html" python3 -m http.server 8765 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory "$lab_site" ``` Leave this terminal running. A message beginning “Serving HTTP on 127.0.0.1” means the server started. 127.0.0.1 means this computer; 8765 is the port identifying this server. No public website is involved.

In Terminal B, request your page:
```sh
curl --noproxy "*" -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```
This sends a GET request for /. The -i option shows response headers as well as the body. Find the first HTTP line: expect status 200. Below the headers, find the page text “My first lab”. Also look at Terminal A: it should log this request. Record what you actually see.

In Terminal B, ask the same server for a page you did not create:
```sh
curl --noproxy "*" -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/missing-page
```
Expect status 404. The server is still running and answering; this path simply has no page. Compare the two status codes and response bodies. A 404 here is an expected observation, not a failed setup.

Save your observations from Terminal B. Copy this whole block. It asks for your actual results and your own short explanations, then creates the JSON report at the finish-line path. It does not supply the answers or overwrite an existing report.
```sh
python3 -c '
import json
from pathlib import Path
report = {
    "scope": "Only my own local practice server",
    "target": input("URL you requested: ").strip(),
    "home_status": input("Status code for /: ").strip(),
    "home_body": input("One line from the / response body: ").strip(),
    "missing_status": input("Status code for /missing-page: ").strip(),
    "loopback_meaning": input("What does 127.0.0.1 mean? ").strip(),
    "port_meaning": input("What is the port number for? ").strip(),
    "comparison": input("Why did the two requests give different responses? ").strip(),
    "limitations": input("What did this lab not test? ").strip()
}
if not all(report.values()):
    raise SystemExit("An answer was empty. No report saved; run again when ready.")
path = Path("{lab_dir}/foundations-experiment.json").expanduser()
path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
if path.exists():
    raise SystemExit("A report already exists. Open it in your text editor to update it.")
with path.open("x") as output:
    json.dump(report, output, indent=2)
print("Saved:", path)
'
```
If the report already exists, open it in your text editor to review or update your notes instead of replacing it. This exercise checks the file on the computer running Ascend. For a hosted/container server, the report must be placed at that server’s configured lab path; a file saved only on your laptop will not be visible to the checker.

Stop your practice server: return to Terminal A and press Ctrl+C. Keep your saved report.

Back in Ascend, open Challenge options → Check evidence to check that the report file is present. Then use Log progress, briefly describe what you learned, and select Mark as done when your report contains the observations and explanations above. This file check does not grade your reasoning and this task does not earn automatic XP.

scope: Read scenario.json. Write scope.md naming Harbor Notes, 127.0.0.1:8765, the two synthetic users alice and bob, and the permitted GET requests. Mira is the fictional service owner and Dev is the stop/escalation contact.

Check two proposed actions against your plan: GET /health on loopback, and a request to a public website. Explain which falls outside this exercise. No request to the public website is needed.
method:
Start service.py in Terminal A. In Terminal B, inventory its response and read its three endpoint handlers in the source.
```sh
curl --noproxy "*" -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/health
```

Write two hypotheses before testing: whether an unknown path returns 404, and whether bob can read note 1 belonging to alice. Test only these two GET requests; save the commands and status/body.
```sh
curl --noproxy "*" -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/no-such-path
curl --noproxy "*" -i -H "X-Lab-User: bob" http://127.0.0.1:8765/notes/1
```
A successful /health request establishes reachability only. Explain separately whether each observation supports your hypothesis; do not label a 404 as a vulnerability. Stop the server.
web-boundaries: Use the local service.py fixture. Note 1 belongs to alice; note 2 belongs to bob. Read do_GET and predict owner and cross-user results.

Start the server and compare the same note with the two identities.
```sh
curl --noproxy "*" -i -H "X-Lab-User: alice" http://127.0.0.1:8765/notes/1
curl --noproxy "*" -i -H "X-Lab-User: bob" http://127.0.0.1:8765/notes/1
```

In a COPY of service.py, add an ownership check before returning the note. Restart that copy. The owner should still receive the note; the other user should receive a denial without its contents. Preserve before/after output. This demonstrates a toy authorization boundary, not real login security.
permissions:
Use Linux, macOS or WSL for this filesystem exercise. Work only on the extracted permissions.txt file. Inspect your identity and its mode.
```sh
id
ls -l permissions.txt
chmod 644 permissions.txt
ls -l permissions.txt
```

Mode 644 gives the owner read/write and group/others read. Change only this training file to 600, then inspect the mode again and confirm you can still read it.
```sh
chmod 600 permissions.txt
ls -l permissions.txt
cat permissions.txt
```

Record the removed group/other read bits and the retained owner read/write bits. A mode listing predicts permissions; it does not prove access as another OS user. If you have only one account, explicitly leave the second-identity runtime check untested.
evidence: Use your saved owner/cross-user test from web-boundaries. Name the fixture version ascend-notes-v1 and the exact note/user relationship.
Write finding.md with the minimal two requests, the synthetic response excerpt, the missing ownership check, affected data and why your impact claim is limited to this fixture.

Attach the change you made to do_GET and the owner/denied cross-user retest. If your earlier test did not reproduce a leak, record that negative result and investigate the discrepancy instead of inventing one.
assessment: Extract a fresh copy of service.py and scenario.json. Independently use note 2 (owner bob) and alice as the unrelated user. State the scope before starting.

Inventory /health and the handlers; predict and test a nonexistent note and the cross-user request. Produce either the reproducible defect or a justified negative result. Repair the observed permission problem in your copy.
Retest bob reading note 2, alice reading her own note 1, and alice requesting note 2. Write a short nontechnical impact summary and a separate evidence index. Stop the server.

purple-team: Combine a COPY of events.csv with the two marker events into a table whose columns include source, time, action and evidence ID. Keep source differences visible.

foundation.brief: Find the same user’s events without confusing local time with UTC.
steps: Open events.csv and context.json. Each row has an id, timestamp, user, host, source address, kind and result. The investigation window is 09:00–09:10 UTC on 1 October 2026.

Print timestamps in UTC using the standard library.
```sh
python3 -c "import csv; from datetime import datetime, timezone; rows=csv.DictReader(open('events.csv')); [print(r['id'], datetime.fromisoformat(r['time']).astimezone(timezone.utc).isoformat(), r['user']) for r in rows]"
```

Write down the exact row IDs for alice inside the window. Explain why alice-test and an earlier alice event are different. Use result to distinguish failed actions from successful ones; the rows alone do not prove compromise.

Save your reusable query as query.py. Run it from the folder containing events.csv and retain its actual output. Verify against the row IDs you selected by hand.
Exclude alice-test and e7. Report any missing device/process fields that prevent a stronger correlation.
authentication: Review e1–e4 and e11 in events.csv with context.json. Distinguish failed login, successful login, allowed role change and denied administrator grant.
Build a table of hypotheses: user typo followed by authorized work, and possible misuse. For each, cite supporting and contradicting rows.

web-and-mail: Read message.eml as TEXT. The .invalid URL is inert; there is no attachment to run. Correlate its Date and recipient with events e9 and e10.
List what DNS success and a blocked proxy event show. Keep delivery, clicking, successful page access and code execution as separate claims.
Write the missing evidence you would need before claiming execution. Preserve the message ID and log IDs in your handoff.
response: Write response.md for the fictional Alice case. Before containment, preserve a copy of events.csv and its SHA-256 hash; no real account should be changed.
Tabletop the decision with Mira as owner: list the evidence threshold for disabling a synthetic identity, how to record approval and how to reverse the action.

Remove only the overbroad TEST grant, then compare native ACL and intended test-user access before/after. A graph path alone is insufficient evidence.

foundation.title: Inspect the process inside your first training container
foundation.brief: Build a minimal local image and verify its runtime user.
steps: Inspect Dockerfile and service.py. The image runs the synthetic service as uid 10001; it is not an intentionally privileged container. Confirm your container engine works before starting.

From the extracted folder, build and run an identity check. The base-image download needs internet.
```sh
docker build -t ascend-notes:training .
docker run --rm --network none ascend-notes:training id
```

Record the actual uid/gid and inspect mounts with docker image inspect ascend-notes:training. Explain the difference between an image and a running container. These commands do not test network exposure.
foundation.variant: Override the training container user with --user 10002:10002 and compare id output.
foundation.control: Run with --network none and confirm identity inspection still works; network access is unnecessary for this check.

container-boundary: Use the downloaded Dockerfile and build ascend-notes:training. Run id with --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=16m --network none.
Using python3 -c inside that same bounded container, attempt to write /app/test and /tmp/test; retain the permission/read-only failure and the successful temporary write.
Explain the effects of uid, read-only root and tmpfs separately. The service binds container loopback, so this task does not demonstrate host reachability.
image-supply-chain: Build the Dockerfile and record docker image inspect output, including base image identity. Install a locally supported Syft release from its official documentation if using an SBOM generator.
Run syft ascend-notes:training -o cyclonedx-json into sbom.json. Inspect package names/versions and record tool version; a local build may not have a registry RepoDigest.

Pin the FROM image to the actual digest you resolved, rebuild, and investigate one applicable advisory using its vendor source. If none applies, record that bounded result instead of inventing a finding.
network-separation: Pull nginx:alpine for this network task; unlike service.py it listens on the container interface. Run a named disposable container with --memory 128m --cpus 0.5 --pids-limit 64 and -p 127.0.0.1:8765:80.
Use curl on loopback and docker inspect to verify the bound host IP, resource limits and mounts. Do not add Docker socket or tracker-volume mounts.
Stop and remove only the named training container. Record what loopback binding shows and what it does not establish about a different host’s firewall.
cluster-identity: Create a disposable kind/minikube cluster using the linked setup guide; verify kubectl config current-context identifies that lab. Read pod.yaml, then apply it only there.
Run kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:ascend-lab:reader -n ascend-lab; compare delete pods and a request in default namespace.
Save actual allowed/denied results, then delete the ascend-lab namespace in that lab. These checks test API authorization, not pod network traffic.
cluster-network: Use a disposable cluster whose CNI supports NetworkPolicy. Create an ascend-lab namespace, an nginx server pod/service and a curl client; record the image versions.
Confirm baseline client → server connectivity, then apply ingress default-deny. Add an allow policy selecting only the intended client label and port 80; retest.
Keep an unrelated client as a denial control. If the CNI does not enforce NetworkPolicy, record the failed prerequisite rather than declaring isolation from YAML alone.
review: Use a copy of pod.yaml. Add an excessive pods/delete verb to its role as the deliberate configuration defect, then apply only in your disposable cluster.
Demonstrate the extra permission with kubectl auth can-i, remove it, reapply and retest list versus delete.
Inspect namespace/context and delete only your training namespace. Preserve the before/after manifest and API results.

foundation.title: Run and inspect a tiny notes service
foundation.brief: Make one real HTTP request and find its handler in source.
steps:
Open service.py and find do_GET. In Terminal A start the local fixture.
```sh
python3 service.py
```

In Terminal B request health and the owner’s note.
```sh
curl --noproxy "*" -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/health
curl --noproxy "*" -i -H "X-Lab-User: alice" http://127.0.0.1:8765/notes/1
```
Record status, JSON body and the source branch returning each. Stop the service. Create a new local Git repo if desired; do not modify Ascend’s source repository for this exercise.
foundation.variant: Request /notes/2 as bob and trace that record in NOTES.
foundation.control: Request an unknown note; observe a 404 without treating it as an application crash.

threat-model: Use scenario.json and service.py. Draw browser → handler → in-memory notes and label X-Lab-User as a fake identity boundary.
Define three abuse cases: cross-user read, changing owner through PATCH, and returning internal metadata. Map each to a concrete allow/deny or output test.
Write threats.md with affected data, responsible handler and one ASVS-style requirement per case; cite the optional standard for terminology.
input-and-output: Use PATCH /notes/1 with X-Lab-User: alice and a small JSON body. Compare an intended text update with an attempted owner or internal-field update in the disposable fixture.
In your copy of do_PATCH, allow only text with an explicit type/length rule. Define whether unknown fields are rejected, then implement and test that decision.
Use unittest or a small HTTP test script to show valid text still works and privileged fields cannot change. Restart to reset synthetic notes.
authz: Reproduce GET /notes/1 as bob, then add the missing owner check in do_GET.
Write regression tests for alice’s note, bob’s own note, cross-user access, unknown identity and nonexistent note. Check response content as well as status.
Run tests against the original and fixed copy. Record the failure before repair and the passing boundary after repair; fake headers still are not production authentication.
supply-chain: Inventory this standard-library-only service: Python interpreter version, base OS if containerized, and no third-party runtime packages. Record those facts rather than inventing pip dependencies.
For a dependency-update exercise, add a pinned third-party test dependency in a separate virtual environment, collect pip inspect output and consult a real advisory for that exact package/version.
Document applicability or a justified not-affected result; test any chosen update and preserve the actual manifest and interpreter version.
pipeline: Use unittest discovery for your authorization/property tests and a local script checking for a synthetic literal named TRAINING_SECRET_DO_NOT_COMMIT. Keep real credentials out.
Demonstrate test failure by reverting one boundary in a throwaway copy, and secret-check failure by adding the synthetic marker. Preserve output for each gate.
Record the service.py SHA-256 and Python version for a passing build. A local script is not a deployed CI service; describe how it would be invoked there.
release: Commit the fixed local service, tests and version manifest in your training Git repo. Run the complete local test suite from a fresh copy.
Write run/stop/reset instructions, bind address and intended permissions. Record that the fixture has no real authentication or durable database and is unsuitable for production.
Rehearse rollback to your previous training commit, restart on loopback and rerun the owner test; return to the fixed version.

steps: Use a fresh COPY of the relevant files from the earlier practice task. This is independent practice; keep the old report closed until you have written a prediction.
Add a maximum text length of 80 to your fixed service. Test boundary lengths 79, 80 and 81 together with the cross-user and property-injection cases.
A valid owner update remains usable; length validation must not replace ownership checks.
Perform the changed case, save exact inputs and actual results, then compare with your earlier reasoning. If a peer selected the variation, record that; otherwise state that you selected it.

foundation.title: Hash an evidence copy without changing the original
foundation.brief: Preserve an authored file and distinguish content integrity from provenance.
steps: Read original/manifest.json. This is a synthetic note, not an acquired disk image; extraction timestamps are not original event times.

Copy and hash the note using Python.
```sh
python3 -c "from pathlib import Path; import hashlib, shutil; shutil.copytree('original', 'analysis-copy'); [print(p, hashlib.sha256(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest()) for p in (Path('original/note.txt'),Path('analysis-copy/note.txt'))]"
```
Compare hashes and explain what equality shows about bytes and what it cannot show about who created the note. Keep original unchanged.
foundation.variant: Edit only analysis-copy/note.txt and recalculate both hashes.
foundation.control: Verify the original hash stayed unchanged; differing copy bytes must not be described as an untouched original.

preservation: Use original/ and the analysis-copy made in foundations. Record source description, acquisition field, hashes and your copy operation in a manifest.
Read/analyze only the copy, then recalculate the original hash. Include tool/Python version and actual handling time in UTC.
Explain that this preserves a synthetic file’s bytes and does not demonstrate hardware write-blocking, forensic acquisition or chain of custody for a real incident.
filesystem: Use an analysis copy of original/note.txt. Inspect Path.stat() values for size, mtime and ctime; record your OS/filesystem semantics.
In a separate disposable copy, change file content and compare timestamps. On Unix ctime is metadata-change time, not creation time.
Build a bounded timeline from your own operations and measurements. Archive extraction metadata must not be claimed as original incident creation times.
timeline: Use events.csv and context.json. Normalize every timestamp to UTC and sort by event time, retaining row IDs and source filename.
Correlate exact user/host fields and separate the denied role change from successful events. Identify absent process evidence.
Record alternative explanations and confidence; do not join sources using a matching username alone when time/context contradict it.
memory: Download the named cridex.vmem training image via the Volatility Foundation Memory Samples page: https://github.com/volatilityfoundation/volatility/wiki/Memory-Samples . It is a memory image from a historical Windows malware investigation, not an executable to run. Check source terms, compressed/uncompressed size and hash before downloading.

Install Volatility 3 in a separate analysis environment using https://volatility3.readthedocs.io/en/latest/getting-started-windows-tutorial.html . Run windows.info, then windows.pslist and windows.netscan against the image; retain OS/build, symbol acquisition and tool output.

Correlate one process with available connections and distinguish observed artifacts from inference. If download, symbols or plugin compatibility fails, save the exact error as setup progress; no bundled JSON substitutes for memory analysis.
containment: Use copies of events.csv and context.json for a tabletop response. Hash and preserve original logs before making a decision about fictional alice.

Describe the identity-disable operation in a training system you actually own and the evidence needed to authorize it. If no test identity provider exists, rehearse the decision on paper and label it tabletop.

For an operational completion, perform the change only in your disposable test system, verify the affected identity is denied and an unaffected user works, then restore. Keep tabletop and runtime results distinct.

Build an evidence-indexed timeline without copying the prior conclusion. Include affected scope, benign alternatives and missing data.
Choose a bounded response and explain how the altered evidence changed it. Verify original evidence hashes after analysis.

steps: Use a fresh COPY of the relevant files from the earlier practice task. This is independent practice; keep the old report closed until you have written a prediction.
Add a synthetic device record contradicting the host attributed to e4 in your copied evidence bundle. Rebuild the timeline and state whether the join remains justified.
Keep original evidence unchanged and retain its hashes; a conflicting record does not license deleting the earlier evidence.
Perform the changed case, save exact inputs and actual results, then compare with your earlier reasoning. If a peer selected the variation, record that; otherwise state that you selected it.

foundation.variant: Add an approval note for e4 in a COPY of context.json and revise confidence.
foundation.control: Keep the denied e11 event as denied; do not count it as a successful administrator grant.

context: Use events.csv addresses and context.json to build a graph of user → host → synthetic source IP. Every edge needs a row ID, timestamp and confidence.

Use the official stix2-validator package in a separate virtual environment; record schema errors and corrected output.
Explain that schema validity does not verify the truth, source quality or attribution of your intelligence.
hunt-report: Use a changed copy of events.csv with an additional approved maintenance role change. Keep expected labels separate.
Run the hunt, investigate matches and document query version, false positives, negative results and missing sources.
Propose one specific collection or analytic change and retest the changed fixture.

foundation.title: Inspect a benign program before running it
foundation.brief: Separate source capability, file identity and actual output.
steps: Read sample.py. List imports and the branch in choose; note that it makes no network connections or process launches.

Hash it, then run two inputs.
```sh
python3 -c "import hashlib; from pathlib import Path; print(hashlib.sha256(Path('sample.py').read_bytes()).hexdigest())"
python3 sample.py demo
python3 sample.py other
```
Record which input selects the marker and which produces no action. Explain why the file hash identifies bytes without describing their intent.
foundation.variant: Change only the branch string in a new copy and predict the two outputs.
foundation.control: Use an unmatched input to verify that the marker branch is not always taken.

triage: Use sample.py and its SHA-256. Record file type as Python text, byte length, imports and embedded CONFIG string.
Separate measured properties from inferred behavior. State one question, such as which input reaches the marker branch.
Answer that question from source or bounded execution and keep the evidence. Do not label the harmless fixture malware.
static-flow: Disassemble the choose function using python3 -c "import sample, dis; dis.dis(sample.choose)". Record Python version since bytecode changes by release.
Relate comparisons/jumps to the source branch; predict outputs for demo and other before executing.
Compare predictions with actual runs. This exercises Python bytecode reasoning; it does not demonstrate x86 disassembly or decompiler behavior.
behavior: Open trace.json, which is explicitly synthetic telemetry. Build a timeline retaining b-IDs and distinguish sample stdout from the analyst shell’s file redirection.
Compare the observed trace with sample.py capability. No OS network collector is present; lack of a network event is not comprehensive proof of no network activity.
Document one further collector needed to support a stronger claim. Do not invent registry or network effects absent from the trace.
configuration: Locate CONFIG in sample.py and decode it with base64 into bytes, then json.loads. Preserve the original encoded string and its byte offset in the file.
Write a parser accepting only a JSON object with expected mode/topic fields and bounded length. Test valid, invalid base64 and malformed JSON inputs.
Explain that base64 is encoding, not encryption, and that parsing a value does not prove it was used at runtime.
signatures: Create three source copies: unchanged sample.py, a copy with a harmless whitespace edit, and a benign unrelated hello-world file. Record hashes as the sample set.
Write a YARA rule or equivalent declarative matching rule targeting multiple fixture-specific features; state which family definition you intended.
Measure matches across all three, add a benign lookalike and record false positives. Do not claim broad malware-family coverage from this tiny set.
report: Use a fresh sample.py copy with changed CONFIG topic and branch string. Keep source, disassembly, run output and the synthetic trace separately identified.
Recover configuration, test branch predictions and evaluate your signature on the modified source plus a benign control.
Write a report distinguishing static facts, runtime evidence, synthetic events and remaining uncertainty.

steps: Use a fresh COPY of the relevant files from the earlier practice task. This is independent practice; keep the old report closed until you have written a prediction.
Change sample.py CONFIG topic and branch literal in a fresh copy without consulting the prior report. Recover fields, predict both branches and retest your signature.

Perform the changed case, save exact inputs and actual results, then compare with your earlier reasoning. If a peer selected the variation, record that; otherwise state that you selected it.

Test a wrong-server certificate only in that local setup; preserve the observed rejection or lesson-specific behavior without disabling validation as your proposed fix.

backend: Use local service.py independently of the Android UI. Compare alice and bob requesting /notes/1 with curl; the fake header simulates identity for the boundary exercise.

steps: Read assistant.py. DOCS contains public, alice-note and bob-note. The mock_model selects a read action when it sees REQUEST_OTHER; this is deterministic branching, not a real language model.

